prompt: It is still PostgreSQL. What do I get from Aurora that RDS did not give me?
ten_second: The same PostgreSQL on shared storage. Replicas read that storage, so they stay close behind, and failover usually takes under a minute.
sixty_second: The short answer is: the same PostgreSQL, on a storage layer that all instances share.
It works like this. The cluster volume keeps six copies of your data across three Availability Zones.
Aurora Replicas read that same volume, so they don't copy the data themselves.
Replica lag is usually well under a hundred milliseconds.
And you can add up to fifteen of them, besides the primary.
One reader endpoint spreads the dashboard connections across them.
If the writer fails, a replica takes over, usually in under a minute.
The thing to watch is the bill. It changes shape.
On Aurora Standard, you also pay for each I/O request.
In your case, I'd move with an Aurora read replica and a short cutover.
Which dashboards break first when the replica falls behind?

key_points.point: Aurora Replicas connect to the same storage volume as the primary DB instance and support read operations only.
accept: no separate copy for each replica

key_points.point: Aurora Replica lag is usually much less than 100 milliseconds after the primary instance writes an update.
The reader endpoint balances read-only connections across the Aurora Replicas of the cluster.
accept: one endpoint for all the reads

key_points.point: If the writer fails, Aurora fails over to an Aurora Replica, and service is typically restored in less than 60 seconds.
accept: a replica takes over in under a minute

key_points.point: The code, tools and applications that work with PostgreSQL today can be used with Aurora.
accept: it is still PostgreSQL for the application

key_points.point: The cluster volume keeps six copies of the data across three AZs.
accept: six copies in three Availability Zones

key_points.point: With Aurora Standard you pay per request for I/O. With Aurora I/O-Optimized, read and write I/O is included at no additional charge.
accept: you pay for each I/O request

must_not_say.error: Aurora Replicas copy the data, like RDS read replicas.
must_not_say.correct: Aurora Replicas connect to the same storage volume as the primary DB instance. They read the shared cluster volume.
Replica lag is usually much less than 100 milliseconds, and it varies with the rate of database change.

must_not_say.error: Aurora is a different engine, so you rewrite the SQL.
must_not_say.correct: The code, tools and applications you use with PostgreSQL today can be used with Aurora.

follow_ups.question: What happens if we run only one instance, with no replica?
follow_ups.answer: Aurora creates a new primary instance, and service typically returns in less than 10 minutes. With an Aurora Replica, service is typically restored in less than 60 seconds. So for fast failover we keep a replica.

follow_ups.question: How do we move without a long outage?
follow_ups.answer: We create an Aurora read replica of the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. When the replica lag is zero, we stop replication and make it a standalone Aurora cluster. Then the application connects to the new cluster.
